request: how does the k-means algorithm group points into clusters?

composition.story: How does k-means group points? Start with six fixed points and two chosen centers. Assign each point to its nearest center, then replace each center with its cluster mean. Watch memberships change while points stay fixed. Finally, test another assignment: unchanged memberships reveal stable clusters.

aha.observation: Both centers equal their cluster means, and another nearest-center assignment changes nothing: the clusters are stable.

parts.presentation: Place below the explanation and above the experiment. Show ordered state labels, the active step, and completed-step trace. Steps represent algorithm states, never elapsed time.

Use the canonical algorithm/collection composition: six fixed point cells above two fixed center cards. Cell positions indicate coordinate order, not distance. Each point cell stacks its name, coordinate, and cluster membership. Center cards identify their seed or mean contributors; center values appear only in readouts. Region phases align with variant.states; select the entry matching the active state. Highlight state.active regions without moving cells. Keep cluster names visible rather than relying on color. Above the experiment, declare one-dimensional coordinates, arbitrary distance units u, fixed k=2, and the displayed initial seeds. Assume nonempty clusters throughout this run. This example demonstrates local convergence, not guaranteed global optimality.
Anchor beside the named active region without covering cells. Show the current action and its reason. Callouts identify where and why; readouts contain numerical results.

Place governing rules above the experiment and bound results below it. Assignment chooses argminⱼ |xᵢ − cⱼ|²; exact ties choose Cluster A. Update cⱼ = Σ{xᵢ : zᵢ=j}/nⱼ, where nⱼ counts assigned points. SSE = Σᵢ(xᵢ − c[zᵢ])², measured in u². Compute results from the active memberships and exact center expressions. Keep exact fractions internally; display centers and SSE to two decimals. Changed memberships compares consecutive assignment passes; initial assignments are identified separately. During mean updates, memberships remain fixed; during assignments, centers remain fixed. Phase supplies the bound status line.

variants.label: Two clusters from six fixed one-dimensional points

states.label: Choose initial centers
states.sentence: P1 through P6 stay fixed; Center A starts at P1, and Center B starts at P3.
states.why: Initial centers are fixed inputs; neither cluster has members yet.

states.label: Assign to nearest centers
states.sentence: Assign P1 and P2 to Cluster A; assign P3 through P6 to Cluster B.
states.why: Each point selects its nearest center; centers remain at their initial coordinates.

states.label: Replace centers with means
states.sentence: Keep memberships fixed; move Center A and Center B to their respective cluster means.
states.why: Mean updates average assigned coordinates, not the previous center positions.

states.label: P3 changes clusters
states.sentence: P3 switches from Cluster B to Cluster A; both centers remain fixed.
states.why: P3 is now closer to Center A because the previous mean update moved Center B away.

states.label: Recompute both means
states.sentence: Center A averages P1 through P3; Center B averages P4 through P6.
states.why: The changed membership changes both cluster means while all point coordinates remain fixed.

states.label: P4 changes clusters
states.sentence: P4 switches from Cluster B to Cluster A; all other memberships remain unchanged.
states.why: The latest center positions make P4 closer to Center A.

states.label: Update means again
states.sentence: Center A averages P1 through P4; Center B averages P5 and P6.
states.why: These mean positions must still pass another nearest-center assignment before declaring convergence.

states.label: Confirm stable clusters
states.sentence: No point switches: Cluster A contains P1 through P4, while Cluster B contains P5 and P6.
states.why: Both centers already equal their cluster means, and every point remains assigned to its nearest center.
